text: The minimum variance portfolio from the last lesson had one clean answer, no worse alternatives lurking somewhere else in the search space. That wasn't luck. It's a property called convexity, and this lesson makes it precise.

A set is convex if the straight line between any two of its points stays inside it. A function is convex if its value anywhere along that line never rises above the straight line interpolation between its endpoints — the graph curves upward or stays flat, never dips below its own chords. For a twice differentiable function, there's a simple test: it's convex exactly when its Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, is positive semi definite everywhere.

Portfolio variance is w transpose sigma w, and its Hessian is just two times sigma, which never changes. A covariance matrix is always positive semi definite by construction, since no variance can be negative. So checking the eigenvalues of sigma confirms directly that portfolio variance is convex everywhere, not just at one candidate point.

That convexity is the whole reason the Lagrangian method could stop at the first stationary point and call it done. For a convex function over a convex feasible set, every local minimum is automatically the global minimum. There's no second, worse basin for gradient descent to get trapped in, and if the function is strictly convex, that minimizer is unique.

Not every natural objective is this well behaved. The Sharpe ratio is expected excess return divided by the square root of variance, and that ratio of a linear term and a square root of a convex term isn't concave in the weights without extra work. Quants handle this with known reformulations rather than assuming every objective is automatically convex.

Convexity is what makes an optimization problem trustworthy rather than just solvable. Up next, lesson twenty seven: quadratic and linear programming, the standard forms that turn convex portfolio problems into something a solver can actually consume.
